query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermo‐mechanical treatment consisting of cryogenic rolling (≈8–10% reduction) followed by low‐temperature annealing will further refine the as‐cast, uniform fine lamellar microstructure of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy, and induce a beneficial phase decomposition/precipitation (e.g., formation of nano‐scale L12-type precipitates) that improves its strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion performance, making it better suited for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term loading, and corrosive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy produced by conventional casting
generation.intervention: Apply cryogenic rolling (approx. 8–10% thickness reduction) followed by a carefully optimized low‐temperature annealing heat treatment (below ~600°C to avoid coarsening)
generation.conditions: Processing performed under cryogenic conditions and annealing temperatures that preserve lamellar spacing; subsequent performance tests under ambient conditions, cyclic thermal exposures up to ~700°C, sustained room-temperature creep loading, and in corrosive test environments (e.g., salt-spray chambers)
generation.structural_mediator: Further refined microstructure with ultrafine recrystallized grains and a controlled degree of phase decomposition/precipitation (e.g., emergence of nano-scale secondary phases at the phase interfaces) within the inherited lamellae
generation.mechanism: The cryogenic rolling introduces a high density of dislocations and refines the grains, while the subsequent low-temperature annealing permits controlled precipitation (and partial phase decomposition) that creates a two-level hierarchy in the microstructure. This synergistically improves the constraint between phases (enhancing the work hardening and resistance to microcracking) and stabilizes the microstructure against creep and environmental attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Tensile yield and ultimate strengths are expected to increase, while ductility and work-hardening capacity are improved; room-temperature creep rates will decrease, and the more stable, refined microstructure should offer better resistance to corrosive environments compared to the as-cast state.
generation.baseline: As-cast uniform fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with strength and plasticity that do not meet industrial fastener requirements.
generation.boundary: Improvements are anticipated within operational temperatures up to ~700°C and under long-term mechanical loading and corrosive conditions; however, if annealing parameters exceed the optimal range (leading to coarsening) or if deformation is overapplied, the benefits may be compromised.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative gains (e.g., percentage increases in strength or ductility) cannot be precisely predicted without process optimization; the optimal balance between recovery and further refinement via annealing is subject to experimental tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: a control group (as‐cast state) and an experimental group subjected to cryogenic rolling (≈8–10% reduction) followed by low-temperature annealing. Conduct a series of mechanical tests (tensile, creep) and corrosion assessments under simulated service conditions including cyclic thermal exposures (ambient to 700°C) and corrosive salt-spray environments.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Creep rate under constant room-temperature loading
Corrosion rate and quality of passive film from salt-spray or immersion tests
Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) to verify refinement and precipitate formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (for example, less than a ~10% enhancement in strength, ductility, or reduction in creep and corrosion rates) relative to the as-cast control, or if undesirable microstructural coarsening or degradation is observed under the test conditions.

cited_evidence.text: These results showed that the yield strength (1437 ± 26 MPa), tensile strength (1562 ± 33 MPa), and elongation (14 ± 1%) of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy after annealing at low temperature were significantly improved compared with the as-cast alloy. Eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit an excellent balance of toughness and strength at room temperature. However, there is still an immediate requirement to design structural components with more strength and ductility due to the increasing technical requirements and harsher operating environments in industrial applications. The demand for stronger and more ductile structural elements has increased as airplane components have become more demanding and technical standards have advanced. Therefore, it is of significance to develop a new eutectic high-entropy alloy with superior properties based on AlCoCrFeNi2.1.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5).
